title: How many people make a shared birthday likely?
answer: A room of 23 people gives a better than even chance that two share a birthday, because 23 people make 253 pairs, each a chance to match

checks.question: Two separate rooms each hold 23 people. When everyone joins one room, how many new pairs become possible, and why can’t you just add the two rooms’ match probabilities?
checks.answer: 529 new pairs: each of the 23 people in one room can now match each of the 23 in the other. The combined room has 1,035 pairs, compared with 506 within the two separate rooms. Adding the old probabilities misses the cross-room pairs and counts overlapping match events twice.

checks.question: On a planet with 100 equally likely birthdays, would 23 people still be needed for a better than even chance of a shared birthday? Use the person-by-person calculation to find the smallest room.
checks.answer: No: 13 people suffice. Multiply the chances of avoiding earlier birthdays, 100/100 × 99/100 × … × 88/100, and subtract from 1: about 55.7%. With 12 people it is about 49.7%. A smaller calendar makes each new pair more likely to match.

steps.caption: A year has 365 days, so a match can seem to need a crowd. Each card is one person. Before searching the dates, guess how likely a shared birthday is in a room this size. This calculation gives every day of a 365-day year the same chance, with independent birthdays and no 29 February.

steps.title: No shared birthday in this room of 10
steps.line: Is that luck, or usual for a room of 10?
steps.caption: Most rooms of 10 have no match: of 1,000 random rooms, 112 had a shared birthday, and the exact chance is 11.7%. A room of 23 people gives a better than even chance that two share a birthday, because 23 people make 253 pairs, each a chance to match. The next steps count those pairs.

steps.title: Your own birthday: only 9 chances to match
steps.line: Predict: how many comparisons does the whole room make?
steps.caption: Mark the first card as you. Each square in the column compares your birthday with one other person’s. You have just one opportunity per person: the chance that someone here shares your birthday is only 2.4%, and an even chance would take 253 other people. But a match elsewhere in the room need not involve you.
steps.picture: You: card 1. card 2. card 10. Comparisons. 9. Chance. 2.4%. Your 9 comparisons, one square each.

steps.title: Every pair drawn: 10 people make 45 pairs
steps.line: Which size of room makes the 253 comparisons you would need alone?
steps.caption: Each newcomer can match everyone already in the room. Each card adds a row with one square for every card before it, building a triangle of 45 pairs instead of your column of 9. No square pairs two cards with the same date in this room. Across all rooms of 10, at least one pair matches with chance 11.7%. A room of 23 makes 253 pairs: enough comparisons for a better than even chance of a match under these assumptions.
steps.picture: Card 1. card 2. card 10. Pairs. 45. Chance. 11.7%. One square per pair: 10 × 9 / 2 = 45.

steps.title: Each newcomer pairs with everyone already in the room
steps.line: The thick bars outrun the thin ones as the room fills.
steps.caption: Each additional person adds one card but a comparison with everyone already present. That is why the thick pair bars grow faster than the thin people bars. Doubling from 5 people to 10 more than doubles the pairs. The bars use one scale; the outlined row is this room.
steps.picture: People. Pairs. Chance. 2. 1. 0.3%. 3. 3. 0.8%. 5. 10. 2.7%. 10. 45. 11.7%. 23. 253. 50.7%. 40. 780. 89.1%. Thin bars: people. Thick bars: pairs, on one scale.

steps.title: Counting exactly: person 10 must miss 9 dates already taken
steps.line: Predict: do 45 pairs at 1 in 365 each give the same chance?
steps.caption: Turn the question around: what would it take for nobody to match? Add people one at a time and ask each to miss every date taken so far. Provided earlier people have all missed, each new arrival has one fewer free date. Multiply those chances to get 88.31% for no match, then subtract from 1: 11.69% for a match. The picture shows the free dates facing person 10.
steps.picture: Person 10: 9 dates taken, 356 free.

steps.title: 45 pairs at 1 in 365 each: about 11.6%
steps.line: Close to the exact 11.69%; overlapping comparisons need care.
steps.caption: Treating the 45 pairs as independent gives the nearby shortcut shown. They are not jointly independent: if Ann matches Ben and Ben matches Cal, Ann must match Cal. The person-by-person calculation avoids that dependence. Comparisons with your one birthday do involve independent arrivals, so multiplying their miss chances gives the exact 2.4% for a match with you.
steps.picture: One pair shares a birthday: 1 in 365. All 45 pairs miss: 364/365, 45 times over. = 88.39% chance of no match. Pair shortcut. 11.61%. Exact. 11.69%. The gap: pairs that share a person.
